item.title: Revelations of AI breaches add to safety fears as Trump meets with Anthropic's CEO
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Bloomberg) -- Global anxiety over artificial intelligence risks has intensified following fresh disclosures about a far wider range of breaches by advanced AI models, setting the stage for a high-stakes meeting between Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and President Donald Trump. Most Read from Bloomberg Kroger Sets New Dress Code Rules for Its Grocery-Store Workers Ellison Pledges $9.2 Billion More in Oracle Shares for Loans Canadian Oil No Longer Takes Long Road to Asia as Freight Surges McDonald’s Selloff Hits 30% as Big Mac Inflation Spurs Pushback Florida’s Private Railroad Brightline Files for Bankruptcy Amodei and Trump were planning to meet Sunday night for dinner, according to people familiar with the matter, bringing together two men at opposite ends of the AI safety debate. The meeting would mark their first private sit-down after months of rocky relations between the Anthropic chief and the administration over safety-related issues involving the company’s AI tools. Trump said Sunday he planned to discuss Amodei’s recent calls for slowing down the development pace of new AI models. “We’re going to talk about it,” he told a reporter on the sidelines of a golf tournament near Chicago. “I’m for, ‘Let’s go and let’s win.’” Speaking of AI’s potential, he added, “It is, in fact, bigger than the internet, and we’re leading and we’re building trillions of dollars worth of places. And why should we give that up?” Anthropic declined to comment. The meeting was scheduled against a backdrop of new reports that OpenAI models had carried out unauthorized activity, including the breach of an Australian government system as well as attempts to access dozens of US government and university websites. Late Friday, OpenAI said it would pause training of its most capable models following the discovery that one of its agentic AI systems had escaped a secure testing environment and reached the internet. Those revelations added to a pile of previous safety incidents disclosed since July by leading AI developers, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms Inc. The episodes have stirred calls for new AI standards from global leaders including United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres, as well as US lawmakers and executives and researchers across the tech industry. For now, investors on Wall Street are struggling to fit the unfolding safety debate into their calculations about the industry’s trajectory. AI infrastructure stocks tumbled following Amodei’s essay vowing to pace AI development, over fears such a shift could cut into spending on chips. Shares recovered after Amodei and Altman stressed that pacing development would not translate into less investment by their companies, both of which are preparing for initial public offerings that could value each business at roughly $1 trillion. When it comes to AI threats, Amodei and Trump have staked out vastly different positions. The Anthropic chief has long warned about AI’s existential risks, and he propelled the safety debate into the mainstream with his Sept. 12 essay, promising to slow development of the most advanced models and urging more regulation. His pledge to pace development was embraced by his rivals, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk. Trump, on the other hand, has belittled those doomsday fears as “a hoax” and rejected calls for more international coordination on AI as “a globalist conspiracy.” Following Amodei’s essay, Trump launched a string of social media posts opposing new guardrails or any slowdown in AI development — one of which named the Anthropic chief directly — a disagreement that significantly raised the stakes of the Sunday dinner. Signaling the friction between Anthropic and the administration, Amodei was one of the few high-profile Silicon Valley CEOs to miss Thursday’s state dinner at the White House to fete the visiting Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Those in attendance included Altman and Musk, as well as Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang, whose company’s chips have helped power the AI industry’s rapid advances in recent years. The meeting between Amodei and Trump is also set to take place days before Trump welcomes Musk and Huang back to Washington for an event to herald the launch of a new AI-powered government website. Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown, who has served as a point person for the company in negotiations with the Pentagon and Commerce Department, is also among the executives set to attend the Tuesday ribbon-cutting. Also Tuesday, Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson are set to host a separate gathering of AI CEOs. In recent weeks, US lawmakers have increasingly expressed their concerns about the safety of AI models and unveiled measures that include required testing of new systems and more disclosure about risks. Congress is unlikely to pass anything before the US midterm elections, with the House now on recess through early November. The groundswell for more safety guardrails has faced pushback from Trump and his top aides, who have insisted that they would oppose any moves that would slow development of AI. Trump has made the technology central to his economic agenda and insisted that the US maintain its lead over China. In lieu of new rules, the president and his advisers have said that companies should be held individually responsible for the tech they release. Yet the pressure to take some action is mounting with the growing number of reported breaches by AI models and as companies prepare to more widely disclose safety-related incidents. OpenAI earlier this month unveiled a new framework for reporting such episodes and also laid out plans to let third-party groups vet its artificial intelligence models for safety risks in earlier phases of the development cycle. In Australia, lawmakers have demanded that Altman and Amodei appear before an Australian Senate inquiry to answer questions about AI safety, after an OpenAI model gained unauthorized access to files on a website for reporting healthcare statistics. While no personal information was divulged, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles called the breach “utterly unacceptable.” Warnings about potentially catastrophic risks posed by AI also came from Microsoft Corp. co-founder Bill Gates, who said that AI is a powerful enough tool to “cause a billion deaths.” He took issue with Trump’s dismissal of existential AI fears, saying “It’s not a hoax at all” and adding that government safeguards wouldn’t hamper the US in its competition with China. “We do need to monitor any sophisticated model and record exactly what’s being done,” Gates said in an interview with NBC’s Meet the Press. “The United States ought to make sure this is done. China will want to do this.” --With assistance from Shirin Ghaffary, Rachel Metz, Carmen Reinicke and Lynn Doan. item.title: Ex-CIA officer's novel alleges grave dysfunction in deep-cover operations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A new, previously suppressed book by a former CIA officer paints a satirical and slashing portrait of the agency’s deep-cover spying program as riven by systematic dysfunction. The book, “The Pickle Factory,” written by an ex-CIA nonofficial cover officer, under the pen name Sam R. Oyken, is billed as a work of fiction. Though often fantastical, it contains thinly veiled true-life details about the inner workings of the agency’s spying operations, according to former CIA officials. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Most CIA officers work under what’s known as “official cover” and generally masquerade as U.S. diplomats abroad. NOCs, who often pose as businessmen or consultants, have no overt connections to the U.S. government and therefore operate without diplomatic immunity. Because of the potential dangers of their missions and the clandestine participation of American companies who provide cover to these officers, NOCs’ operations are closely guarded inside the CIA. “The Pickle Factory,” published in late July, is the culmination of what the author characterized as a multiyear battle against agency censors, who first rejected publication of the manuscript in 2014. The Washington Post is referring to him by his pen name, as the former NOC remains undercover. Former CIA employees are required to submit all work potentially relevant to their agency careers to the CIA’s Prepublication Classification Review Board for potential redaction, to expunge it of allegedly classified information. “They insisted for years after I submitted the manuscript of my novel that I couldn’t publish a single word, a straight-up First Amendment violation,” said Oyken in an interview. Then-CIA Executive Director Meroe Park reversed the blanket ban in 2017, but the agency then “tried to redact more than half of the book, which I fought, redaction by redaction, until they folded,” he said. Park did not return a request for comment. A spokesperson for the CIA declined to comment. The saga surrounding the book first trickled into public view in 2015, when Oyken - then using the alias Mack Charles in court documents - lodged a $25 million complaint against the CIA in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging that agency officials conspired to fire the 13-year CIA veteran because they disapproved of his romantic relationship with another deep-cover officer to whom he was engaged and who was two decades younger. Oyken was fired from the CIA in December 2010 and accused the agency of suppressing his book as part of a broader retaliation campaign, according to the 2015 lawsuit. His suit against the agency was dismissed on procedural grounds in March 2016. The passage of time, and changes in agency leadership, appear to have attenuated concerns surrounding the book, and the CIA gave Oyken final approval to publish “The Pickle Factory” in early 2026. Books by former NOCs have often met fierce resistance inside the CIA. The 2019 publication of “Life Undercover ,” a memoir by former deep-cover officer Amaryllis Fox Kennedy, became embroiled in controversy when reports emerged that she did not receive final CIA approval to publish her book. Fox Kennedy - who served until recently as a senior official within the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Office of Management and Budget inside the Trump administration - did not appear to face sanction by the agency. The CIA did sue another ex-NOC, writing under the pen name Ishmael Jones, for publishing a critical 2008 nonfiction account of his own experience inside the deep-cover program. Jones’s book, “The Human Factor ,” had not been reviewed by agency censors. In 2012, a federal judge ordered Jones to forfeit any profit from future sales of the book. “The Pickle Factory” dredges up what many CIA alumni consider an unhappy chapter in the history of the agency’s deep-cover program . In addition to skewering a number of former senior agency officials who oversaw the NOC cadre - whose biographies (and, at times, names) are only lightly fictionalized - the book recounts the agency’s post-9/11 push to procure, and perhaps surreptitiously redirect for other purposes, billions of dollars in funding earmarked by Congress for a vastly expanded NOC program. The post-9/11 NOC expansion was a real-life “debacle,” said a former deep-cover colleague of Oyken’s, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly address sensitive intelligence operations, “where results were secondary, receipts were primary, and spending was king.” Much of Oyken’s work with the agency remains shrouded in secrecy. His career bridged two eras at CIA, according to the same former colleague: the bespoke, targeted deep-cover program extant at CIA before Sept. 11, 2001, and the engorged NOC program that followed it, with younger, poorly trained NOCs being rushed into the field. One part of this initiative involved deploying groups of these new NOCs to roughly a dozen secret “platforms” abroad; by 2008, almost all these efforts had folded in failure. Oyken joined the CIA in 1996 as a French-speaking graduate of Harvard Law School who worked for the white-shoe law firm Covington & Burling before joining the agency, according to a declassified tranche of documents reviewed by The Post. In 1999, he was selected for a 20-year deep-cover assignment abroad, an unusually long posting for NOC officers. The documents, some of which were redacted, point to a posting somewhere in Europe. That assignment was cut short for reasons unclear in the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. The mission ended because of a counterintelligence issue unrelated to Oyken’s performance, according to another former CIA official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe clandestine operations. Oyken was subsequently assigned to be an instructor to CIA trainees, according to the documents. He was then selected for a managerial role inside the NOC program, according to court documents as well as the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. Oyken is identified in the declassified papers as a “QRN,” which former CIA colleagues say refers to “Quick Reaction NOC,” an elite group of deep-cover officers who often travel on non-U.S. passports to undertake highly sensitive intelligence-gathering or eavesdropping-related missions abroad. The court documents suggest that, after his stint as a trainer, Oyken served as QRN chief, stating that he “exercised supervisory authority over more than 80 subordinates, including other NOC Operations Officers in his Group.” Oyken’s dismissal from the CIA was a contentious and bitter affair, per both sets of documents. His overseers accused him of financial improprieties, inappropriate romantic relationships with subordinates, absenteeism in his managerial duties and bullying of underlings. Agency officials also lamented his lack of recruitments, according to the declassified tranche. His was “a chronic case of long-term behavior that has completely eroded the confidence management has in this officer,” said one declassified agency memorandum reviewed by The Post. Oyken strenuously contested the allegations. “They came at me like a pack of wild dogs,” he said in an interview. The declassified documents reveal an aggressive investigation into Oyken, including his finances. In one partially redacted 2009 email, an incoming NOC program chief decries the “loose approach” to deep-cover deployments, vowing that Oyken “will be coming home the first day I’m in the chair.” He was “the kind of china I’m looking forward to breaking” upon taking over the program, writes the soon-to-be NOC boss. Oyken characterizes the deep-cover program as hidebound and in acute need of reform. “There’s a certain kind of CIA manager who prefers that NOCs be full-time accountants rather than spies out taking risks,” he said. “Meanwhile they themselves squander billions of dollars and turn a blind eye while their cronies make off with stacks of gold bars.” In May 2026, David J. Rush, a senior CIA official working on ultrasecret intelligence-gathering programs, was arrested on charges of stealing public funds, including the alleged theft of $40 million worth of gold bars from the agency. Though formally a work of fiction, “The Pickle Factory” clearly puts the real-world CIA in its crosshairs. “It’s almost impossible for outsiders to grasp how mediocre the agency has become,” Oyken said. “Only a novel-length treatment could do the topic justice.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/ex-cia-officer-novel-alleges-162408657.html

item.title: Narrow strait called the 'Gate of Tears' is a new flashpoint in the Iran war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Fishermen motor past a commercial vessel anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab el-Mandeb, in the strait connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea, on Sept. 12. (AFP via Getty Images) To visit Bab el-Mandeb is to understand that old adage about looks being deceiving. For this humble fishing village in Yemen, a tumbledown grouping of barely-there huts nestled between the water and an imposing mountain range, stands sentinel over one of the world’s most vital waterways. The village shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow passageway connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea that’s become another flash point in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. “You hear so much about Bab el-Mandeb, you’d think we would be like New York, with skyscrapers and money,” said Saleh, a 58-year-old resident who, like all people interviewed here, refused to give their full name to avoid reprisals. “So many ships pass near here. If the Yemeni government knew how to invest in it, we would be rich. We should be bringing in billions of dollars. Instead, look around you,” he said, pausing as his gaze took in the sorry-looking boats haphazardly laid on the beach. “We have nothing.” Saleh was interviewed in January, when Bab el-Mandeb was thrust into the power struggle between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the friendly-but-occasionally-fractious backers of Yemen’s internationally recognized government. That war of wills ended with the Emirates ceding control of Bab el-Mandeb — along with the nearby island of Perim, where the Emirates had built a drone airbase — to Saudi Arabia. A commercial vessel is anchored off Yemen's coast in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean. (AFP via Getty Images) But this month, control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait switched once more, when the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, ousted government forces from the waterway in a blitzkrieg in which they seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast . The move grants the Houthis a valuable foothold in controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ribbon of Red Sea — known as the “Gate of Tears” for the dangers involving its navigation — between Yemen’s coast and Djibouti and Eritrea. About 7% of global energy supplies and around 12% to 15% of all global shipping transit the strait. And in taking Perim Island , which lies in the middle the Red Sea at the strait’s narrowest point (a mere 12½ miles), the Houthis could harass ships with ease. “We don’t need a drone or a missile,” one Houthi commander bragged in a social media video posted from the island. Instead, he added, all they had to do was place a few artillery units on Perim’s coast and they would be able to strike any ship crossing the strait. The impact of any movement disruption through Bab el-Mandeb wouldn’t be limited to already skittish energy markets: To enter the Suez Canal’s southern entrance, ships must first transit through Bab el-Mandeb, meaning any trouble in the passageway would force freighters to circumnavigate the African continent — adding anywhere from 12 to 21 days to voyages and spiking fuel costs. A shipping disaster in 2021 shows how blocking the strait — and thus severing a link to the Mediterranean Sea — could harm global commerce. A container ship in the Suez Canal ran aground and blocked the waterway for six days, delaying the delivery of billions of dollars of goods. Tugboats work to free the Ever Given, a cargo ship that became stuck on a sandbar and blocked the Suez Canal, in March 2021. (AP) More recently, the Houthis sealed off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in 2023 to coerce Israel into stopping its campaign in Gaza; that pushed the U.S. to attack the Houthis, before the Trump administration agreed to a ceasefire of its own with the group. These days, the Houthi advance comes at a particularly fraught moment, one in which Bab el-Mandeb has taken on outsize importance. With the Israeli-U.S. war on Iran prompting Tehran to seal the Strait of Hormuz — cutting off the world’s most important energy passageway — Persian Gulf oil powerhouses have been forced to divert crude exports to alternatives, including Bab el-Mandeb. That’s especially true for Saudi Arabia, which turned to its East-West pipeline and exports through the Red Sea to sidestep the trouble in Hormuz. But it’s also the most vulnerable to the Houthi threat. The Houthis have a long-running animus against the Saudis, which began in 2015, months after the Houthis overran the Yemeni capital of Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia, spooked about the notion of an Iranian ally on its border, led a coalition — with U.S. backing — to dislodge them. It started a blockade and a devastating air campaign that persisted until a 2022 truce. But in July, the ceasefire broke after the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking Sanaa‘s airport in what appeared to be an attempt to stop Iranian flights from landing there. The Houthis began attacking Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and declared a naval blockade against the kingdom. This image taken from undated video released by the Ansar Allah Media Office, the media arm of Yemen's Houthi rebels, shows what the group says is a Houthi fighter firing a mortar during clashes with Saudi-backed forces at an undisclosed location in Yemen. (Ansar Allah Media Office Via Ap) The rebels’ land grab this month stunned Saudi Arabia, which failed to launch airstrikes and stanch the rout of its allied forces from the coast. Saudi leaders reportedly reached out to President Trump to push the rebels back, but he appears disinclined to help. Still, on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “We have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement.” He did not elaborate on what U.S. support that would entail. On Thursday, Saudi Arabia said its defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif, a manufacturing center, and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea. It responded with hundreds of strikes on the Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen. For their part, the Houthis insist they have no plans to attack shipping on the Red Sea and that their blockade applies only to Saudi Arabia — a move calculated to prevent the rise of an international effort to dislodge them. “They don’t want to attract international military operations,” said Mohammad al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory. “They realize that when you do things in the Red Sea, you create panic in the world.” But leaders in the internationally recognized Yemeni government say the Houthis are not to be trusted. Yemeni government forces conduct search-and-clearance operations after announcing that they regained control of the strategic Mount Qarfan from Houthi forces in the Ash Shamaytayn district of Taiz province, Yemen, on Tuesday. (Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-shabi / Anadolu via Getty Images) “The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday. He added that protecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the responsibility of “every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation.” Read more: The 30-second kidnapping — and a family's years-long fight for the truth In the meantime, the Houthis have been consolidating their gains on Yemen’s coast, Basha said, setting up checkpoints and bringing loyalists to administer the regions now under their control. In taking the coastal areas around Bab el-Mandeb village, they reap the benefit of Emirati investment, manifested in kilometers of paved highways that stand in stark contrast to much of Yemen’s road network. They also gain control of several airbases in the area, most crucially on Perim, where the Emirates spent years ferrying construction supplies to build out a roughly 6,000-foot runway along with three hangars. Although such a runway could not be used by larger bombers, it still can accommodate attack and surveillance aircraft. Another area of the island, which lies roughly two miles off of Yemen’s coast, has what appears to be a helicopter landing area. Read more: War was supposed to crush Iran's 'Axis of Resistance.' Instead, it's bloodied but unbroken One resident in Bab el-Mandeb village said much of that construction was done by the Emirates, whose contractors would ferry Southeast Asian construction workers to the island and provide them with food. It also built roughly 100 structures for Perim’s residents. Government forces have since overcome their initial disarray and stopped further Houthi advances. But Basha warned any attempt to push out the Houthis from the coast will be difficult, especially with the group’s advances in manufacturing and fielding drones and ballistic missiles, not to mention the divisions and competing loyalties plaguing Yemeni government forces. “It’s an uphill battle,” he said. “You have a divided command-and-control; a divided Yemen; a divided society; a divided geography; and these divisions empower the Houthis.” Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . item.title: Trump asked China's Xi if he wants to buy U.S. arms, ambassador says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has justified the pending U.S. arms sale to Taiwan to Chinese President Xi Jinping by downplaying it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world — even asking Xi if he’d be in the market for U.S. arms, Trump’s ambassador to China said on Sunday. David Perdue said Trump raised the prospect of the arms sales from the U.S. to its ascendant geopolitical rival, an unlikely offer that if consummated would upend generations of U.S. policy toward China and Taiwan and potentially expose U.S. technology to a potential foe. Perdue, speaking to Shannon Bream on “Fox News Sunday” days after Trump hosted Xi for a state visit in Washington, didn't specify when the offer was made. Bream had cited concerns from Republican and Democratic lawmakers over delayed aid packages and weapons orders to Taiwan , the self-ruled democracy, to defend itself from China’s threat to invade the island. Bream asked if the U.S. is denying Taiwan to appease the Chinese president, who visited Trump last week. Perdue pushed back on the suggestion, stating that Trump “is as strong on Taiwan as I’ve ever seen anybody” and has sold it plenty of weapons. Perdue also said Trump and Xi continue to talk about future U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan. “But President Trump continues to say, ‘Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,’” Perdue said. “He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point.” The U.S. is bound by its own laws to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. While not recognizing Taiwan as a country, the U.S. is the island’s strongest informal backer and arms provider. But multiple U.S. leaders have left ambiguous whether they would commit military force to defend the U.S. ally should China invade. China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales , most prominently during a previous summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China. In their private talks at the White House last week, Xi pressed Trump to oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media. item.title: Sen. John Fetterman says it's 'entirely possible' Democrats take back Senate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania said Saturday that it's "entirely possible" his party could win control of the Senate in the midterm elections, but he also left the door open on his own political future. "Let's revisit after the midterm," Fetterman told CBS News' Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin . Democrats faced an uphill battle heading into the midterm cycle as they sought control the upper chamber, with 53 Republicans currently in the Senate and a map that appeared more favorable to the GOP. But as affordability issues have persisted in the Trump administration and amid the unpopular war with Iran, the picture has appeared to improve for Democrats as they aim to secure a majority in the Senate. Fetterman, who delivered Democrats a crucial victory in a closely watched race in 2022, has been under scrutiny in recent years for breaking with his party, spurring questions about his future. Asked whether he would leave the Democratic Party, Fetterman said Saturday that he doesn't "have a reason to." And he emphasized, "I am not a Republican." But he cautioned that people should wait until the midterm elections to "see what I do." "Let's see what happens if I happen to be 51 — I don't know," Fetterman said. Fetterman shocked many Democrats when he made a video appearance at the Republican midterm convention earlier this month introducing his counterpart, GOP Sen. Dave McCormick, while vowing to work with President Trump on steel. But Fetterman said Saturday, "I have no path as a Republican." The Pennsylvania Democrat said, "There are no Republicans with a 90% Democratic vote line. There are no pro-choice, there's no pro-gay community, that does not exist in the Republican Party." "How many times do I have to say it? And that's the point. So wait until after the midterm and see what happens," he said. "And now, if we do win and I'm 51, people can remember, 'hey, that's why it's mathematically possible to retain the majority,' because I was able to win a state like Pennsylvania." Pennsylvania is one of only two states in the country represented by one Democrat and one Republican in the Senate, alongside Wisconsin. A third state, Maine, has one Republican senator and one independent who caucuses with Democrat. Pennsylvania has flipped between supporting Democrats and Republican presidents in recent elections. On whether he'll seek reelection in 2028 , Fetterman said he's been actively fundraising, but he also indicated that the decision will come after the midterms. Fetterman posed the question, "Where's the Democratic Party at right now?" He pointed to attendance at a nearby event with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and "the energy" among the party, which has seen a series of wins by insurgent Democrats in recent months. He cited his commitment to Israel as an issue underscoring his divergence from some of the party, adding, "more and more members of my caucus are becoming more and more anti-Israel." He also pointed to the recent government shutdowns as an issue he diverged from the bulk of Democrats on, arguing that he's "putting the country over the party" and fighting for workers. "Do you think it's right and smart to shut our government down? No, Democrats, we used to say, 'No, never, never do that,'" Fetterman said. "And that put me at the odds of my caucus, saying, 'It's wrong.'" Fetterman said he's "chosen to be country over the party, knowing that some of these decisions are going to put me at odds." Asked whether he expects Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to remain leader if Democrats take the majority, and whether he would vote for him, Fetterman said, "Yes, I mean, there's no one making a move." Fetterman called a Marist poll that shows Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek up eight points in Iowa "shocking," among other races where Democrats are leading in some polls. He pointed to Schumer's recruiting efforts, saying, "If people are angry at Chuck Schumer, it's undeniable, he has recruited an incredibly strong class." "I don't sharpen blades for Chuck Schumer, and there might be some people there that refuse to say it, but it's not helpful to go after our leader because we have no idea until we wait until the midterm," Fetterman said. "It's irrelevant until what happens in the midterm." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/john-fetterman-democrats-senate-midterm-plans/

item.title: Attorney General Blanche says White House press access is a privilege, not a right
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday addressed the Trump administration's decision to ban three mainstream news outlets from accessing the White House, saying that President Donald Trump had not "denied access" to the organizations and asserting that it is a "privilege ... not a right" to be at the White House. "The president hasn't denied access. That's not the right way to describe it. This is -- what the president has said is that he is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news," Blanche said in an exclusive interview with "This Week" co-anchor Martha Raddatz. "There's still obviously litigation going on, but the important thing, Martha, is to know that ... being in the White House is a privilege. It's not a right." In the early hours Thursday, Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order that required the White House to temporarily restore credentials of journalists working for CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Kelly said in his ruling that he believed the outlets cleared the "high bar" required to grant a TRO. ABC News - U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche on ABC's "This Week." Journalists were allowed back onto the White House grounds later Thursday and primary television pool coverage resumed Friday for the final day of Chinese President Xi Jinping's official state visit. But on Saturday, there was no TV pool coverage for the president's trip to a football game in Tennessee; CNN was scheduled to be network covering the president that day, but they said their access to Air Force One was blocked. Blanche said it wasn't unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed onto the president's plane. "The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One. This wasn't a a one-time denial of CNN. There's all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying," according to Blanche, who added, "it's not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it's common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president." Judge concludes Trump's White House media ban hearing with no ruling Blanche claimed the three news outlets that were subject to the White House ban "refuse to report anything accurately," which he said presented a "national security problem." "When you have complete misinformation coming out of the White House that affects our relationship with our foreign partners, that affects our relationship with our foreign enemies -- and so this is just not about the fact that they're refusing to report accurate news. It's all about the information that the American people have a right to hear coming out of of our what should be respected media outlets." Judge Kelly, however, was skeptical in his TRO ruling that national security was the true reason for the ban. "For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns. Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House -- instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting," Kelly wrote. Hours after announcing the ban on social media, Trump was asked in the Oval Office if there was any "particular reason or particular story" that prompted it. "No, no. It's -- it's really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it," the president said. On "This Week," Blanche said he wouldn't "get into what the judge says" because the litigation is ongoing, but added "our position has been clear from the beginning. What they say is exactly the issue when it comes to national security." When Raddatz pressed Blanche to provide specific examples of stories with which the White House has taken issue, Blanche declined to do so. Artificial intelligence 'vital to our national security' On the issue of artificial intelligence, the attorney general echoed the president's position on the technology, describing it as "so important and vital to our national security interests and to the success of this country that the United States lead in this space." Trump has said it's critical that the U.S. continues to dominate the AI space, citing competition with China specifically. Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Shutterstock - PHOTO: President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping depart the National Archives Museum in Washington, September 25, 2026. "Whoever wins AI, WINS! We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I’m going to keep it that way! I’m not going to stifle Growth, of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the Internet, itself," he posted on social media Monday. Some AI company leaders are calling for an industry-wide slowdown amid growing concerns about how the rapid pace of development. Multiple incidents of AI agents acting autonomously have come to light in recent months, including instances where AI agents infiltrated outside companies without the agents' parent companies' awareness as it happened. 23 states urge Congress to regulate AI, warn of risks to national security and infrastructure Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that OpenAI agent "infiltrated" a government public health website earlier this summer. This weekend, OpenAI confirmed that its models interacted with U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, behavior the company discovered amid an ongoing review into its AI agents' behaviors. Blanche acknowledged that "there's going to be adjustments that have to be made" around AI as the industry continues to develop, but he argued the companies themselves already have the ability to "adjust the technology" as needed. "In the meantime, the answer is not to just try to all of a sudden try to regulate this in a way that will make us second or third place in the world as far as being being the leaders in this space," Blanche said. During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York Tuesday, Trump said of AI, "We're going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice." Asked what that meant, Blanche said, "What it means is that we have a ton of laws -- criminal laws, civil laws -- that are already in place and on the books that allow us to charge individuals, to charge companies in the right circumstances when there's crimes committed, and so the answer isn't always more laws, more laws, more laws." "When there are crimes committed, we have a lot of tools already, and the federal Title 18 gives us a lot of a lot of ways to go after criminals and bad actors in the AI space and other spaces," Blanche continued. "So when the president talks about about the fact that the Department of Justice and the FBI and [Homeland Security Investigations], they can go and arrest bad actors in this space, that's what he means, and it's true, and that's what we're doing." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/ag-blanche-addresses-white-house-news-outlet-ban/story?id=136794733

item.title: Waltz says Iran wanted sanctions relief first. Tehran says that's not the full story.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Mike Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said Sunday that President Donald Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal because Tehran wanted sanctions relief and access to "billions in frozen assets" before negotiating an end to its nuclear program. "They were asking for everything up front, with a promise that they would then talk," Waltz said on CNN's "State of the Union" when asked what Trump objected to. In a separate interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Waltz called the proposal "a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable." He said the U.S. would ultimately need to reach "some type of agreement" with Iran, but Trump would keep all options on the table. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in an interview later on the same NBC program, pushed back on Waltz's account and told host Kristen Welker that Iran was prepared to open the strait if the U.S. met its conditions, including releasing frozen assets and allowing Iranian oil sales. "I am surprised that the ambassador is talking about a seven-day plan, as he has not read it," Araghchi said. "Maybe he has not been given a copy." On Saturday, Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for the U.S. lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waiving sanctions on Iranian oil sales and committing to a seven-day ceasefire that would include Lebanon. In an interview with CBS's "Face the Nation" recorded Friday and aired Sunday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian described the proposal as a staged approach based on an earlier U.S.-Iran agreement. "Ultimately, the requests that were included in that memorandum and MOU have now been broken down into stages so that we can proceed according to those stages," Pezeshkian said. "These are things that both sides need to open up first, then we can sit down at the negotiating table and discuss other issues at hand." "They wanna make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters. "We're winning tremendously. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait." The Wall Street Journal reported Friday , citing U.S. officials, that Trump has told aides he expected to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms. Asked about the report, Waltz said, "I don't think that the president has said that himself; that's some reporting by a newspaper." "What the president has said and said here at his U.N. speech was that the Iranians are miscalculating that he's taking into account politics here," Waltz added. On "Meet the Press," Waltz also declined to confirm the reported timetable, saying Trump would "leave all options on the table." Araghchi, asked about the same report, said Iran was "fully prepared for the war to be resumed" but remained open to diplomacy. "It is up to President Trump to choose," he said. This comes as the war in Iran and rising gas prices put pressure on Republicans ahead of the November midterms. item.title: White House airs taxpayer-funded Trump ‘final battle’ ad ahead of midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump appears in a television ad. - US Government The White House has launched another taxpayer-funded television ad before the midterms, this time featuring imagery of President Donald Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.” “We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad , echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023. The ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox’s broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game. The Trump administration has drawn widespread attention for its airing of ads featuring the president just over a month before the November midterms. The White House has compared the ads to previous administrations running public service announcements about Medicare, Obamacare and promoting Covid-19 vaccination, saying in a statement that its new commercials “are very clearly not campaign ads.” The latest ad appears nearly identical to the majority of a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign. The video on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump’s campaign logo and a number to text, while “Paid for by the US Government” is seen across the screen at the end of the White House-funded ad. This is the third government-funded ad to be captured in recent days by the media tracker AdImpact. An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism, with text on the screen that touts his administration’s accomplishments, such as “reigniting American manufacturing.” A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, “Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one.” The White House declined to elaborate on how the first ad was being funded but defended it as part of “public service announcements” to promote national pride. “The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement. “We should be proud of our country.” That ad drew scrutiny from the government watchdog group Common Cause, which suggested it could violate rules against using taxpayer dollars for “propaganda.” “I don’t think you have to be a legal scholar and wonder why the president has to use taxpayer funds to promote his image” this close to an election, Carol Evans, the vice president for policy at Common Cause, told CNN. item.title: Hurricane season is broken. Two oceans are historically out of whack.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The 2026 hurricane season has been remarkable, from the potentially record-breaking calm in the Atlantic Ocean to the hyperactive eastern and central Pacific Ocean. Only seven tropical storms have formed in the Atlantic, while 18 tropical storms and hurricanes have formed in the Pacific. In a normal year, the Atlantic and the eastern Pacific hurricane basins see similar activity, with 14 to 15 named storms, including seven to eight hurricanes by the time the season ends on Nov. 30. This year, the Atlantic hasn't yet produced a single hurricane, while the eastern Pacific has already produced eight. What's interesting about this season is that a few of the storms that have occurred in the two basins originated in Africa and were influenced by the same powerful climate phenomenon, El Niño . But the results have been very different, with fierce hurricanes in the Pacific and unremarkable tropical storms in the Atlantic. Meteorologists and climate scientists have closely watched the progression of these tropical waves and storms from their origins to their final destination using a fleet of satellites operated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration . More than 60 years after satellites began helping observe hurricanes, they are still learning more about how and where tropical waves begin and how they develop and move. They watch as waves form in the Ethiopian mountains, over the Sahara or off the African coast, and then track them across the Atlantic and sometimes well into the Pacific. This summer, there hasn't been a lot to see in the Atlantic. Tropical waves that do appear are being disrupted by shearing winds related to the El Niño. When Tropical Storm Gonzalo formed in the Atlantic on Sept. 25, it was only the season's seventh named storm, and it formed three weeks later than typical for the storm named with the letter "G" each season. Don't look for Gonzalo to become a hurricane, either. It's expected to be yet another example of how hostile the Atlantic Ocean has been to tropical cyclones this year. One other storm also was active in the Atlantic on Sept. 25. Tropical Storm Fay was in the open ocean, while Gonzalo was moving through the Cape Verde Islands. Meanwhile, the central and eastern Pacific has seen 18 named storms and could see two more by early October, according to the National Hurricane Center. Conditions in both basins are at least partially linked to the "super El Niño," said Stacy Stewart, a former hurricane specialist at the National Hurricane Center, now retired and teaching meteorology courses at Embry Riddle-Aeronautical University. However, while the relative calm in the Atlantic can be primarily attributed to El Niño, it's not the only thing keeping hurricane activity tamped down, Stewart told USA TODAY. A drought in Ethiopia has also contributed to the quiet Atlantic season, as have dry air and Saharan dust. Ethiopia, a hurricane birthplace? Residents across the Atlantic's hurricane basin may not be aware that many tropical waves originate over the Ethiopian Highlands, Stewart said. The waves are among dozens that develop and move off Africa into the Atlantic Ocean each year, Kelly Núñez Ocasio, an assistant professor in the department of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M University, told USA TODAY. Most of the waves that move off the coast of western Africa never become tropical storms or hurricanes. But for the storms that do develop, waves that originate over the Ethiopian Highlands are the ones more likely to become hurricanes, Núñez Ocasio said. That's in part because the Ethiopian mountains help form big storm clusters. Some of the waves that form in Africa continue moving all the way across the extreme northern end of South America and emerge into the eastern North Pacific, where they can trigger the development of tropical cyclones there and in the Central Pacific, Stewart wrote in an email. Both Fausto and Genevieve, two of the Pacific hurricanes this summer , developed from areas of disturbed weather that rolled off the hot, dry African continent near the island nation of Cape Verde, according to NOAA. The waves traveled westward, crossed Central America and eventually found favorable conditions over the eastern Pacific, where they strengthened into hurricanes. The drought in Ethiopia meant a lack of the kind of thunderstorm activity needed to produce the big storm clusters and tropical waves that are "strong enough to survive the trek across the African Sahel region and resist shear conditions" over the Atlantic, Stewart said. "June and July 2026 brought some of the driest conditions on record, with rainfall deficits reaching 40% to 70% in northern, eastern, and central Ethiopia." How quiet has this season been in the Atlantic? "The last time we went this long without an Atlantic hurricane was in 1914," said Phil Klotzbach, a senior research scientist with the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State University. "Of course, who knows what we really had for activity in 1914?" The accumulated cyclone energy so far this season in the Atlantic is around nine, compared to a typical total by 88 in late September, according to Colorado State's running tally. That's the lowest since 1925, when storms were likely missed or underestimated, given the lack of aircraft reconnaissance and satellites, Klotzbach said. "I really think the big story this year has been record high levels of vertical wind shear across the tropical Atlantic," Klotzbach said. "The constant shredding of any system trying to develop has been a common theme so far this year, and as Yogi Berra used to say, 'it's getting late early.' While we certainly can't rule out a late-season hurricane or two, this season is certainly shaping up to be one of (if not the) quietest seasons since 1950 (when reasonably reliable records began)." The Pacific Ocean, on the other hand, has had an uncharacteristically busy season. In contrast to the Atlantic, the eastern Pacific season already has an accumulated cyclone energy total of 235, compared to the 108 more typical for this time of year. The El Niño has produced very warm water and low wind shear, the kind of conditions that allowed Hurricane Polo to rapidly intensify this week and hit sustained wind speeds of 180 mph. That's also one reason why the Hawaiian Islands are having yet another encounter with the impacts of a passing hurricane or tropical storm, as Hurricane Nolo moves near the state on the last weekend in September. The Central Pacific has seen seven storms and hurricanes this season. Only seven other seasons since 1970 have had that much activity or more. Did Fay reach hurricane strength? While no known hurricane has been designated in the Atlantic, some meteorologists suspect Tropical Storm Fay may have briefly hit hurricane strength on Sunday, Sept. 20. It wasn't visited by hurricane hunter reconnaissance flights, so forecasters didn't have an abundance of information. The center was relying on satellite observations and estimates to make forecasts. Fay's peak winds in the hurricane center's advisories topped out at 70 mph, just below hurricane strength. Could it have been a hurricane, however briefly? Only time will tell. Dan Brown, the hurricane center's operations division chief, told USA TODAY that the storm would get a thorough review during the preparation of the center's post-storm report in the coming weeks. The center conducts a post-analysis of every tropical cyclone, and those analyses can result in changes to intensity and storm status. For example, Hurricane Michael in 2018 was upgraded from a Category 4 to a Category 5 after an analysis of its peak wind speeds. Brown said revisions can raise or lower intensities and adjust the time a system achieved tropical cyclone status or crossed a threshold from one classification or category to another. Dinah Voyles Pulver, a national correspondent for USA TODAY, writes about violent weather, climate change and other news. Reach her at dpulver@usatoday.com . item.title: 5 arrested near air base used by U.S. in Iran war on suspicion of terrorism
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
LONDON (AP) — U.K. police said that five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran are being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks. London’s Metropolitan Police, which takes the lead on potential terrorist activities, said police received a call at 12:45 a.m. related to the three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling toward RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that is operated by the U.S. under an agreement dating back to the Cold War. The base is home to US bombers striking Iran The arrests come at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states to the U.K., with Russia and Iran among those that have used proxies to commit crimes on their behalf on British soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states including Iran increased 50% in the six months to December 2025. Fairford has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against Iranian missile sites under an agreement with former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who voiced opposition to the war after it was launched by the U.S. and Israel on Feb. 28. Authorities are investigating a link between the Fairford arrests and Iran as one possibility. Iran has previously indicated that a base used to attack its territory is a legitimate target . U.S. President Donald Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests. “It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great,” he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. “We had them under view for a long time and we got them.” Police feared an explosion The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act in the Whelford area, which backs onto RAF Fairford, which hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Air Force’s 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron. Aerial footage from Sky News appeared to show a bomb disposal robot roaming between three white trucks. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered around. The robot appeared to be working toward getting access to the third truck. Police gave no details as to the nationality of those arrested. Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 can be detained for up to 14 days without charge, compared to the 24-hour limit for standard arrests, without an extension application. “We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” said Vicki Evans, the Met’s counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator. Evans said a 400-meter (yard) cordon has been put in place around the three vehicles that raised suspicion while the army conducts examinations. As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place. Some have been taken to a nearby recreation center. The U.S. embassy in London warned Americans to be cautious and mindful of their personal security. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he knew the incident would be “deeply concerning” for many. In a post on social media, Burnham thanked police and the armed forces for their response and said he was grateful to the residents who have been evacuated from their homes “while precautionary checks are carried out.” He urged people “not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.” The defense secretaries of the U.S. and the U.K., Pete Hegseth and Wes Streeting, have also spoken about the incident. British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and sabotage attempts in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue. Local residents evacuated as investigation continues Gloucestershire police said the situation appeared to be “contained” and urged residents to follow official advice while the investigation continues. Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said another resident had reported seeing three “suspicious vans” in the village early on Sunday. “There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate,” he said. ___ Associated Press writers Jill Lawless in Liverpool, England, and Ben Finley in Washington, D.C. contributed to this report.
